investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What is the role of ANA in autoimmune serology?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: The screening test for connective tissue disease (especially SLE). It is sensitive but non-specific (also positive in healthy/elderly people), so a positive ANA prompts titre/pattern and specific antibodies (ENA, dsDNA).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Which antibody is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Anti-dsDNA — specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis. (Anti-Sm is also highly specific.)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How do ANCA subtypes map to the vasculitides?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• cANCA / anti-PR3 → granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
  • pANCA / anti-MPO → microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) and eosinophilic GPA (EGPA)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Compare rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP in rheumatoid arthritis.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• RF is non-specific (also Sjögren's, healthy people)
  • Anti-CCP is specific for RA and prognostic (erosive disease)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Which autoantibodies point to primary biliary cholangitis and autoimmune hepatitis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• AMA (anti-mitochondrial) → primary biliary cholangitis
  • ASMA (type 1) and anti-LKM (type 2) → autoimmune hepatitis

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: When is the ENA panel sent, and what does anti-Ro/anti-La indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: After a positive ANA. Anti-Ro (SSA)/anti-La (SSB) → Sjögren's (also SLE). Anti-Ro crosses the placenta → neonatal lupus / congenital heart block.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Which ENA antibody is highly specific for SLE?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Anti-Sm (Smith) — highly specific for SLE (though present in only a minority).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How do anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere distinguish scleroderma subtypes?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Anti-Scl-70 → diffuse systemic sclerosis (lung fibrosis, renal crisis)
  • Anti-centromere → limited systemic sclerosis / CREST (pulmonary hypertension)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What does anti-Jo-1 indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Polymyositis / dermatomyositis — part of the antisynthetase syndrome (interstitial lung disease, mechanic's hands, Raynaud's).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Which antibody is associated with mixed connective tissue disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Anti-U1-RNP (high titre) is characteristic of mixed connective tissue disease.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Why do anti-Ro-positive pregnant women need extra monitoring?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital complete heart block — so fetal cardiac monitoring is arranged.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How do anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor differ in rheumatoid arthritis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Anti-CCP is specific for RA, prognostic (erosive disease) and can precede symptoms
  • RF is sensitive but non-specific (also Sjögren's, other CTD, infections, healthy elderly)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Give non-RA causes of a positive rheumatoid factor.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Sjögren's (high titre)
  • SLE and other connective tissue disease
  • chronic infections (infective endocarditis, hepatitis C)
  • sarcoidosis
  • and healthy elderly people

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What does anti-CCP positivity imply for RA prognosis and management?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Worse prognosis — erosions and extra-articular disease — warranting earlier, more aggressive DMARD therapy. Combined RF + anti-CCP positivity carries the highest risk.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Does a negative RF and anti-CCP exclude rheumatoid arthritis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: No — seronegative RA exists (~20–30%). RA is a clinical diagnosis; serology supports but does not exclude it.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Why should RA treatment not wait for serology?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: RA is a clinical diagnosis and early DMARDs prevent irreversible joint damage — refer persistent synovitis urgently rather than delaying for antibody results.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What three antibody tests are used to diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Lupus anticoagulant
  • anticardiolipin (aCL)
  • and anti-β2-glycoprotein I
(IgG/IgM). Persistence on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart is required.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Explain the lupus anticoagulant paradox.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: It prolongs the APTT in vitro (and does not correct on mixing) but causes thrombosis, not bleeding, in vivo.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What are the clinical (Sydney) criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Vascular thrombosis (arterial/venous) or pregnancy morbidity (recurrent miscarriage, late fetal loss, severe pre-eclampsia), plus a persistently positive antiphospholipid antibody ≥12 weeks apart.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Give clinical clues to antiphospholipid syndrome.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Recurrent VTE/arterial thrombosis (stroke in the young)
  • recurrent miscarriage
  • thrombocytopenia
  • livedo reticularis
  • an unexplained prolonged APTT
  • and a false-positive syphilis serology

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How is antiphospholipid syndrome managed?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Thrombosis → lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin (DOACs less effective, especially triple-positive)
  • Pregnancy → aspirin + LMWH

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What do C3, C4 and CH50 assess?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: C3 and C4 are individual components consumed in immune-complex disease. CH50 (total haemolytic complement) tests the whole classical pathway — a very low/absent CH50 screens for a component deficiency.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What does a low C3 AND C4 indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Consumption via the classical/immune-complex pathway — classically active SLE (complement tracks disease activity and lupus nephritis). Also cryoglobulinaemia, MPGN, endocarditis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: What does a low C3 with a NORMAL C4 suggest?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: Alternative-pathway activation — classically post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (or a C3 nephritic factor in MPGN).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: Which complement finding points to hereditary angioedema, and how is it confirmed?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back: A persistently low C4 is the screening clue to C1-inhibitor deficiency; confirm with a C1-inhibitor level and function.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How do early-classical vs terminal complement deficiencies present?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
• Early classical (C1, C2, C4) deficiency → an SLE-like disease (poor immune-complex clearance)
  • Terminal (C5–9/MAC) deficiency → recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infection

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.front: How is suspected rheumatoid arthritis investigated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.back:
RA is a clinical diagnosis supported by:
  • RF and anti-CCP (anti-CCP more specific + prognostic)
  • inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP)
  • and imaging — X-ray of hands/feet for erosions, or ultrasound for synovitis.
These feed the ACR/EULAR criteria; refer early to rheumatology for DMARDs.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is HLA-B27 and how should a positive result be interpreted?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: An MHC class I allele associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies. It is present in ~8% of healthy people, so it supports a diagnosis but does not confirm it (and a negative does not exclude).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Which conditions are associated with HLA-B27 (mnemonic)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
PAIR:
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis (strongest, ~90%)
  • IBD-associated (enteropathic) arthritis
  • Reactive arthritis
— all seronegative (RF/ANA negative).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What are the shared extra-articular features of the spondyloarthropathies?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Enthesitis
  • dactylitis (sausage digit)
  • anterior uveitis
  • aortic regurgitation
  • and apical lung fibrosis (in AS)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the reactive arthritis triad?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'), typically following a GI or genitourinary infection.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What features suggest inflammatory (rather than mechanical) back pain?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Onset <45 years
  • worse at rest / better with activity
  • morning stiffness >30 min
  • and waking in the second half of the night
— suggesting axial spondyloarthritis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What disease is HLA-B51 associated with, and what is its hallmark?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Behçet's disease — a systemic vasculitis whose hallmark is recurrent oral (and genital) ulceration. HLA-B51 supports the (clinical) diagnosis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: List the key clinical features of Behçet's disease.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Recurrent oral ulcers (required)
  • genital ulcers
  • uveitis
  • skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pathergy)
  • arthritis
  • and GI/neurological/vascular involvement (VTE, aneurysm)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the pathergy test?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: A papule or pustule forming after a needle prick to the skin (non-specific skin hyper-reactivity) — characteristic of, and supportive for, Behçet's disease.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Where is Behçet's disease most prevalent, and how is major-organ disease treated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
Along the Silk Road (Turkey, Middle East, East Asia).
  • Mucocutaneous disease → colchicine
  • major-organ involvement → corticosteroids and immunosuppression (azathioprine, biologics)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Give the classic HLA class I disease associations.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• B27 → ankylosing spondylitis/spondyloarthropathies
  • B51 → Behçet's
  • A3 → haemochromatosis
  • Cw6 → psoriasis

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What diseases are associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• DR3: SLE, Sjögren's, Graves', autoimmune hepatitis, coeliac, Addison's, T1DM
  • DR4: rheumatoid arthritis, T1DM
  • DR3 + DR4 together → highest T1DM risk

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the clinical value of HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing in coeliac disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Coeliac is almost always DQ2 or DQ8 positive, so the test has a high negative predictive value — a negative DQ2/DQ8 makes coeliac very unlikely (used to exclude, not confirm).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Which diseases are linked to HLA-DR2/DR15?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Goodpasture's disease
  • narcolepsy
  • multiple sclerosis
  • and SLE
Narcolepsy's DQB1*06:02 is the strongest known HLA–disease association.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Why should most HLA associations be treated as supportive rather than diagnostic?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: The alleles are common in the general population and only modestly raise risk — the notable clinically useful exception is the high NPV of DQ2/DQ8 for coeliac disease.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is matched between donor and recipient in transplantation?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: ABO compatibility and HLA-A, -B and -DR (the most important loci) — better HLA matching means less rejection and longer graft survival.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What does the transplant cross-match detect, and what does a positive result mean?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: It detects preformed recipient antibodies against donor HLA (from prior transfusion, pregnancy or transplant). A POSITIVE cross-match is a contraindication — it predicts hyperacute rejection.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Compare hyperacute, acute and chronic graft rejection.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Hyperacute (mins–hrs): preformed ABO/HLA antibodies → thrombosis; prevented by cross-match
  • Acute (weeks): T-cell ± antibody-mediated → treat with immunosuppression
  • Chronic (months–years): fibrosis/vascular change

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the panel reactive antibody (PRA)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: The % of the population the recipient has HLA antibodies against — a high PRA means highly sensitised and harder to find a compatible donor.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Which transplant carries a graft-versus-host risk, and how does immunosuppression trade off?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Bone-marrow/stem-cell transplant (and non-irradiated cellular blood in the immunocompromised) risks GVHD. Maintenance immunosuppression prevents rejection but over-suppression risks opportunistic infection and malignancy.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Why is HLA-B*57:01 tested before starting abacavir?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: It predicts a severe abacavir hypersensitivity reaction. A positive result means do not prescribe abacavir — a pre-prescription pharmacogenetic screen (used in HIV care).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Which antibodies are tested in myasthenia gravis, and how common is each?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-AChR (acetylcholine receptor) — positive in ~85% of generalised MG (main test). Anti-MuSK in many AChR-negative cases; a minority are seronegative.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of myasthenia gravis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back:
Fatigable weakness worse with activity / towards the end of the day —
  • ptosis
  • diplopia
  • bulbar (dysphagia/dysarthria)
  • proximal limb and respiratory weakness

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Which investigations support a diagnosis of MG (besides antibodies)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back:
• Repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response)
  • single-fibre EMG (most sensitive)
  • the ice-pack test
  • and CT chest for a thymoma

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: How is myasthenia gravis managed, including a crisis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back:
• Pyridostigmine (symptomatic) + immunosuppression (steroids, azathioprine) ± thymectomy
  • Myasthenic crisis (respiratory failure) → monitor FVC, ICU, IVIG or plasma exchange

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Which drugs can worsen myasthenia gravis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers (and others) — avoid, as they can precipitate a crisis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What antibody and cancer are associated with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-VGCC (P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel) antibodies — reducing presynaptic ACh release. ~50–60% are paraneoplastic, associated with small-cell lung cancer.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: How does LEMS weakness differ from myasthenia gravis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: LEMS causes proximal (leg) weakness that IMPROVES with repeated use (post-tetanic potentiation) and reflexes that return after exercise — the opposite of MG's fatigability; ocular/bulbar signs are less prominent.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What autonomic features occur in LEMS?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Dry mouth, constipation and impotence — reflecting reduced autonomic cholinergic transmission.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What does repetitive nerve stimulation show in LEMS?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: An INCREMENTAL response at high frequency (or after exercise) — the opposite of the decrement seen in myasthenia gravis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What must be actively excluded in a patient with LEMS?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Small-cell lung cancer — LEMS may precede the cancer by months to years, so screen (CT chest ± PET) and re-screen if initially negative.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What is the defining antibody of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and what does it target?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG) — it targets the astrocyte water channel. Anti-MOG defines a related but distinct entity (MOG-antibody disease).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What are the hallmark clinical features of NMOSD?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back:
• Optic neuritis (often severe/bilateral)
  • longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 vertebral segments)
  • and area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups/vomiting)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: How does NMOSD differ from multiple sclerosis on CSF and imaging?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back:
• NMO has longitudinally extensive cord lesions and CSF oligoclonal bands usually NEGATIVE
  • MS has shorter cord lesions, typical brain lesions, and positive oligoclonal bands

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Why is it important to distinguish NMOSD from MS before treatment?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Several MS disease-modifying drugs (e.g. interferon, natalizumab) can worsen NMO. NMO is treated with steroids/plasma exchange acutely and immunosuppression (rituximab and NMOSD-specific biologics) for prevention.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: How is an acute NMOSD relapse treated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: High-dose corticosteroids and plasma exchange; long-term relapse prevention uses immunosuppression (rituximab, eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab) — not MS drugs.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What antibody and clinical triad define Miller Fisher syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-GQ1b antibodies; the triad is ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia. It is a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What infection classically precedes Miller Fisher syndrome / GBS?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Campylobacter jejuni (also CMV, EBV) — a post-infectious immune-mediated neuropathy.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What is the characteristic CSF finding in GBS / Miller Fisher syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Albuminocytological dissociation — a raised CSF protein with a normal cell count.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: How is Guillain-Barré syndrome (including Miller Fisher) managed and monitored?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: IVIG or plasma exchange, with supportive care; monitor FVC (respiratory failure) and autonomic function. Miller Fisher generally has a good prognosis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: A young woman has a viral prodrome then psychosis, seizures and orofacial dyskinesias with autonomic instability. Diagnosis and antibody?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis — anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies. Test CSF (more sensitive than serum). Same “antibody → hunt the tumour” logic as MG/LEMS.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Once anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis is confirmed, what tumour must you screen for and how?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: An ovarian teratoma — pelvic / transvaginal USS ± MRI pelvis (CT abdo/pelvis if needed). Tumour removal plus immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG/PLEX, rituximab) is the treatment.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: What is the key rule about oligoclonal bands when diagnosing MS?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: They must be CSF-restricted — present in the CSF but absent from a paired serum sample (intrathecal synthesis). Always send CSF and serum together; matched bands indicate systemic inflammation, not MS.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.front: Which antibody marks the axonal (AMAN) variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.back: Anti-GM1 antibodies — the acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) variant, classically post-Campylobacter. (Anti-GQ1b = Miller Fisher.)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the target of anti-GBM antibodies, and what disease do they cause?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Type IV collagen (α3 chain) in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes → Goodpasture's (anti-GBM) disease: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What does renal biopsy immunofluorescence show in anti-GBM disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Smooth LINEAR IgG deposition along the GBM (contrast with granular deposits in immune-complex GN).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the classic clinical syndrome of Goodpasture's disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
A pulmonary-renal syndrome:
  • rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis with haematuria/AKI
  • plus pulmonary haemorrhage (haemoptysis, worse in smokers)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What additional antibody should be checked in anti-GBM disease and why?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: ANCA — around 30% are double-positive (anti-GBM + ANCA), which affects prognosis and management.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: How is anti-GBM disease treated, and why urgently?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Urgent plasma exchange (removes antibody) plus immunosuppression (steroids + cyclophosphamide). Renal recovery is poor once oligoanuric/dialysis-dependent, so treat early.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What does anti-PLA2R indicate, and how common is it?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: It is the marker of primary membranous nephropathy (a leading cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults (especially older Caucasian patients)), positive in ~70–80% of primary cases (anti-THSD7A in a smaller subset).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What are the biopsy findings and secondary causes of membranous nephropathy?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
Biopsy: subepithelial immune deposits ('spike and dome', thickened GBM). Secondary causes:
  • malignancy
  • SLE (class V)
  • hepatitis B
  • and drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: How is anti-PLA2R used clinically?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• A positive result supports primary MN and is used to monitor disease activity/response and predict relapse
  • a negative result should prompt a search for a secondary cause (including malignancy)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Why is nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous) prothrombotic?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Urinary loss of antithrombin III (and other factors) creates a hypercoagulable state → high risk of VTE and renal vein thrombosis; consider anticoagulation in high-risk patients.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the first-line immunosuppressive approach for high-risk primary membranous nephropathy?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Rituximab is now the preferred first-line immunosuppressant (KDIGO), alongside supportive care (ACEi/ARB, diuretics, statin); treat any secondary cause.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Which post-streptococcal antibody is most useful after a SKIN infection (impetigo/pyoderma), and why?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Anti-DNase B. ASO is often poorly raised after skin infections, whereas anti-DNase B rises reliably — so it is the better marker following pyoderma/impetigo. Send both to maximise diagnostic yield.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the typical latent period and complement pattern in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Nephritic syndrome appearing ~1–2 weeks after throat or ~3–6 weeks after skin infection. C3 is LOW and normalises by ~6–8 weeks (C4 usually normal).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: How does IgA nephropathy differ from PSGN in timing and complement?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• IgA nephropathy is 'synpharyngitic' — haematuria occurs WITHIN 1–2 days of the infection with NO latent period and a NORMAL C3
  • PSGN has a latent period (1–6 weeks) and a LOW C3 that recovers

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What are the classic clinical features and renal biopsy findings of PSGN?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
Clinically:
  • visible 'coca-cola'/smoky haematuria
  • hypertension
  • oedema
  • AKI/oliguria
  • mild proteinuria
Biopsy: subepithelial 'humps' on EM with granular IgG/C3 on immunofluorescence.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Why is a single raised ASO titre of limited value, and what is more useful?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Titres remain elevated for months and healthy children can have raised baselines, so one value only proves past exposure. Rising/paired titres (acute + convalescent samples 2–4 weeks apart) are far more informative for confirming a recent GAS infection.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the two-tier serological algorithm for Lyme disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Screening ELISA first; if positive OR equivocal, confirm with an immunoblot (Western blot). A positive ELISA is never sufficient alone — the immunoblot provides specificity.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Why can Lyme serology be falsely negative in early disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Antibodies take weeks to develop (the "window"). In the first few weeks serology may be negative despite active infection — repeat in 4–6 weeks if suspicion persists.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Can Lyme serology be used to confirm cure or diagnose reinfection?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: No. IgG antibodies persist for years after successful treatment, so serology cannot monitor treatment response or reinfection. It is a diagnostic test, not a test of cure.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: How is erythema migrans diagnosed and managed?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: It is a CLINICAL diagnosis — treat empirically with doxycycline without waiting for serology, which is frequently negative this early.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: First-line and alternative antibiotics for Lyme disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Doxycycline first-line
  • amoxicillin as an alternative (e.g. pregnancy/children)
  • ceftriaxone (IV) for CNS involvement (neuroborreliosis) or Lyme carditis

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: Match the ANCA pattern/antigen to its vasculitis: c-ANCA/PR3 vs p-ANCA/MPO.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• c-ANCA / anti-PR3 → granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
  • p-ANCA / anti-MPO → microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) & eosinophilic GPA (EGPA)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What is the renal biopsy picture and next step in ANCA-associated GN?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Pauci-immune crescentic GN — few/no immune deposits on immunofluorescence (unlike linear anti-GBM or granular lupus). Urgent steroids + cyclophosphamide/rituximab; plasma exchange if severe renal failure or pulmonary haemorrhage. Check anti-GBM too (~30% double-positive).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What serology and immunofluorescence pattern characterise lupus nephritis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Anti-dsDNA high
  • C3 AND C4 both low (classical-pathway)
  • ANA positive
Biopsy graded ISN/RPS class I–VI; immunofluorescence is “full house” (IgG/IgM/IgA/C3/C1q).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: What urine microscopy finding indicates glomerular (nephritic) bleeding, and how is proteinuria quantified?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Red-cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs = glomerular bleeding. Quantify protein with ACR or PCR on a spot sample; nephrotic-range ≈ PCR >300–350 mg/mmol (~>3.5 g/day).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: A child has palpable purpura on the buttocks/legs, colicky abdominal pain, arthralgia and haematuria. Diagnosis and its renal link?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) — the systemic form of IgA nephropathy (same mesangial IgA on biopsy), usually post-URTI. Mostly supportive; monitor urine dip & BP for renal involvement.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: How does the complement pattern help localise the cause of a glomerulonephritis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back:
• Low C3 + low C4 = classical/immune-complex → lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinaemia, endocarditis
  • Low C3, normal C4 = alternative pathway → post-strep GN (recovers 6–8 wks) and C3 glomerulopathy/MPGN (persistent — biopsy)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.front: A patient has palpable purpura, arthralgia and MPGN with a markedly low C4. What is the diagnosis and the key next test?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.back: Cryoglobulinaemia — RF positive, cryoglobulins positive, disproportionately low C4. Strongly linked to hepatitis C → send HCV serology and treat the virus.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Which antibody is the marker of autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: TPO antibodies (anti-thyroid peroxidase). High in Hashimoto's hypothyroidism and often also positive in Graves'.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is TRAb and what disease does it cause?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: TSH-receptor antibody — a stimulating antibody that activates the TSH receptor, causing Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism). Used to confirm Graves' when the cause of thyrotoxicosis is unclear.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Why must TRAb be measured in a pregnant woman with Graves' disease, even if she is now euthyroid?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: TRAb crosses the placenta and can stimulate the fetal thyroid, causing fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis. This risk persists even after definitive treatment (surgery/radioiodine), so TRAb is measured and the fetus monitored.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What does TPO antibody positivity predict in subclinical hypothyroidism?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
• Higher risk of progression from subclinical to overt hypothyroidism
  • and increased risk of post-partum thyroiditis

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Do thyroid antibodies replace TFTs for diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: No — they support (explain the cause of) the biochemical diagnosis but must be interpreted alongside TSH and free T4; they do not replace TFTs.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Which autoantibody is the marker of autoimmune Addison's disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Anti-21-hydroxylase (21-OH) antibodies — directed against the adrenal steroidogenic enzyme; positive in the majority of autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency, the commonest cause of Addison's in the developed world.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What test diagnoses adrenal insufficiency itself (as opposed to anti-21-OH defining the cause)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: The short Synacthen test — a subnormal cortisol rise after synthetic ACTH. Supported by a low 9am cortisol and a high paired ACTH (indicating primary disease). Anti-21-OH then confirms it is autoimmune.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is the classic electrolyte pattern in Addison's disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia (from mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency), often with hypoglycaemia. Hyperpigmentation results from high ACTH.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Autoimmune Addison's belongs to which syndromes, and what conditions associate with it?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS-1 and APS-2). Associations:
  • type 1 diabetes
  • autoimmune thyroid disease
  • coeliac disease
  • pernicious anaemia and vitiligo

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: How is an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis managed, and what are the sick-day rules?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus IV 0.9% saline — do not wait for results. Sick-day rules:
  • double the usual oral glucocorticoid dose during acute illness or fever
  • carry a steroid emergency card and IM hydrocortisone

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is the first-line serological test for coeliac disease?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG IgA) — high sensitivity and specificity. Total IgA must be measured at the same time.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Why must total IgA be checked when requesting coeliac serology?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Selective IgA deficiency is over-represented in coeliac disease and causes false-negative IgA-based serology. If IgA is low, use IgG-based tests (IgG anti-tTG / IgG-DGP / IgG-EMA).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What dietary condition must be met for coeliac serology (and biopsy) to be valid?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: The patient must be on a gluten-containing diet — gluten in more than one meal per day for at least 6 weeks. A gluten-free diet normalises serology and biopsy, causing false negatives.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is the confirmatory/more specific second-line antibody test after a positive or weak anti-tTG IgA?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA IgA) — more specific than tTG, used to confirm.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is the gold-standard confirmatory investigation for coeliac disease in adults, and its key histological features?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
Duodenal biopsy (on a gluten-containing diet):
  • villous atrophy
  • crypt hyperplasia
  • and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Which antibodies and which C-peptide result confirm autoimmune Type 1 diabetes?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Anti-GAD (best in adults), anti-IA2, anti-ZnT8, islet-cell antibodies, with a low C-peptide. A preserved C-peptide points to Type 2 / MODY.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Once autoimmune Type 1 diabetes is confirmed, which associated autoimmune conditions should you screen for?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
• Coeliac disease (anti-tTG + total IgA)
  • and autoimmune thyroid disease (TFTs / anti-TPO)
— they cluster with T1DM.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: How do the serology and LFT patterns differ between autoimmune hepatitis and PBC?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
• AIH = hepatitic (raised ALT, raised IgG) with ASMA/ANA or anti-LKM1; biopsy shows interface hepatitis
  • PBC = cholestatic (raised ALP, raised IgM) with AMA (M2)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: A patient has cholestatic LFTs, is AMA-negative and has ulcerative colitis. Which diagnosis and next test?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) — associated with UC/IBD, often pANCA positive; next test MRCP showing “beaded” multifocal strictures.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: Contrast anti-intrinsic-factor and anti-parietal-cell antibodies in pernicious anaemia.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
• Anti-intrinsic-factor = highly specific (diagnostic) but less sensitive
  • Anti-parietal-cell = sensitive but non-specific

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: What is the abnormality pattern and next step in autoimmune gastritis / pernicious anaemia?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back: Macrocytic anaemia with low B12 and hypersegmented neutrophils. Confirm B12, then OGD — atrophic gastritis with increased gastric cancer risk.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.front: In thyrotoxicosis with negative/equivocal TRAb, what does a radioisotope uptake scan show?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__E.back:
• Diffuse high uptake = Graves’ disease
  • low/absent uptake = thyroiditis (de Quervain’s, postpartum) or factitious thyroxine

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: On SPEP, how do you distinguish a polyclonal from a monoclonal gammopathy, and what does each imply?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Polyclonal = broad-based rise across the whole gamma region from many clones → reactive/benign (chronic infection, liver disease, autoimmune)
  • Monoclonal = single discrete narrow spike from one clone → paraproteinaemia (MGUS, myeloma, Waldenström's, amyloidosis) requiring further work-up

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What is immune paresis and why does it matter in myeloma?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Suppression of the uninvolved (background) immunoglobulin classes by the malignant clone, giving low IgG/IgA/IgM outside the paraprotein. It causes increased infection risk and supports myeloma over MGUS.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A patient has a monoclonal IgM paraprotein. Which condition and which emergency complication should you think of?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia. The large pentameric IgM causes hyperviscosity syndrome (headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, confusion) — treated urgently with plasmapheresis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What does the CRAB acronym stand for in myeloma end-organ damage?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• hyperCalcaemia
  • Renal impairment
  • Anaemia
  • Bone lesions (lytic)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: After SPEP detects a paraprotein, which two further tests complete the paraprotein screen, and what does immunofixation add?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Serum free light chains
  • and urine Bence Jones protein
Immunofixation types the paraprotein into its heavy and light chain (e.g. IgG kappa), confirming clonality.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What is the key readout of the serum free light chain assay, and what does an abnormal value indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: The kappa:lambda (κ:λ) ratio (normal ~0.26–1.65). A skewed ratio indicates a clonal excess of one light chain, suggesting a monoclonal process such as myeloma or AL amyloidosis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why can serum free light chains detect myeloma that serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) misses?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: In light-chain-only and non-secretory myeloma the clone produces only free light chains and no intact immunoglobulin, so SPEP shows no paraprotein/M-spike. The sFLC assay directly quantifies the clonal free light chains, revealing disease that electrophoresis misses.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why must a modified (renal) reference range be used for the κ:λ ratio in renal impairment?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Free light chains are renally cleared, so in CKD both κ and λ rise and the ratio shifts upward (κ accumulates relatively more). A renal reference range prevents over-calling clonality from this non-clonal rise.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What renal complication is caused by filtered monoclonal light chains, and how does it present?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney") — light chains precipitate in the tubules causing acute kidney injury. Hypercalcaemia contributes; these are part of the CRAB features (hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why is the sFLC assay a better monitoring marker than SPEP after treating myeloma?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Free light chains have a very short serum half-life (hours) versus weeks for intact IgG, so sFLC levels change rapidly and reflect treatment response much faster than the paraprotein on SPEP.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What tests make up the full myeloma screen?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)
  • immunofixation
  • serum free light chains (sFLC)
  • and urinary Bence Jones protein (urine electrophoresis/immunofixation)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What is the screening test for hereditary angioedema (HAE), and how does it behave between attacks?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Serum C4. It is characteristically LOW both during and between attacks, so a persistently low C4 is a useful first-line screen; a normal C4 during a symptomatic attack makes HAE very unlikely.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Distinguish HAE type 1 from type 2 on complement testing.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Type 1 (~85%): LOW C1-INH antigenic level AND low function
  • Type 2 (~15%): NORMAL or raised C1-INH level but LOW function
Both have low C4 and normal C1q.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: How do you distinguish hereditary from acquired C1-INH deficiency?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: C1q. It is NORMAL in hereditary HAE but LOW in acquired C1-INH deficiency (which is associated with lymphoproliferative/autoimmune disease, has later onset and no family history).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why doesn't HAE respond to adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids, and what is used instead?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: HAE angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated, so standard anaphylaxis drugs are ineffective. Acute treatment is C1-INH concentrate or icatibant (a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Which common drug class is contraindicated in HAE and why?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: ACE inhibitors — they block breakdown of bradykinin, potentiating it, and can precipitate or worsen angioedema attacks. They should be avoided lifelong.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A paraprotein and CRAB features are confirmed on screening — what are the definitive next investigations?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Bone marrow aspirate & trephine (clonal plasma cells ≥10%) and whole-body MRI or low-dose CT for lytic lesions (skeletal survey is now superseded).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What are the classic first clues to myeloma on routine bloods and film?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Normocytic anaemia
  • rouleaux on the blood film
  • a very high ESR/plasma viscosity
  • and raised total protein (high globulin, low albumin)
— these prompt the SPEP.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why can a standard urine dipstick be negative in myeloma, and what should you request instead?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: The dipstick detects albumin only, not free light chains — so it can be negative despite heavy Bence-Jones proteinuria. Request urine electrophoresis / immunofixation; a normal dipstick does NOT exclude myeloma kidney.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Give two practical consequences of selective IgA deficiency.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• (1) False-negative IgA-based coeliac serology — use IgG-based tTG
  • (2) Risk of anaphylactic transfusion reactions from anti-IgA antibodies — give washed / IgA-deficient blood products

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A patient with monoclonal free light chains has nephrotic syndrome or a restrictive cardiomyopathy. What is suspected and how is it confirmed?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: AL amyloidosis (macroglossia, periorbital purpura; often no SPEP band). Confirm with a Congo red biopsy (fat pad/rectal/renal) showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What does a transient rise in serum mast cell tryptase indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Mast-cell degranulation — it retrospectively supports/confirms anaphylaxis or mast-cell activation. It is a confirmatory test, not a reason to delay adrenaline (anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: List the three timed tryptase samples in suspected anaphylaxis.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• (1) As soon as possible after resuscitation has started (do not delay treatment)
  • (2) 1–2 hours after symptom onset (peak)
  • (3) baseline ≥24 hours later or in convalescence to confirm return to baseline

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Does a normal tryptase exclude anaphylaxis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: No. Tryptase can be normal in anaphylaxis, especially food-triggered or normotensive reactions. Drug/venom triggers and hypotensive reactions more reliably raise it.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What does a persistently elevated BASELINE tryptase suggest?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: An underlying mast cell disorder — systemic mastocytosis or hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia — warranting allergy/immunology referral.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What supports anaphylaxis on serial tryptase results?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: A dynamic rise-and-fall: a peak at 1–2 hours that returns to the patient's own baseline by ≥24 hours, rather than a single absolute value.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What defines a positive skin prick test?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: A wheal ≥3 mm larger than the negative (saline) control, read at 15 minutes. A positive (histamine) and negative (saline) control are both mandatory.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Why is 'sensitisation ≠ clinical allergy' the key concept in allergy testing?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: A positive SPT or specific IgE only shows the patient has made allergen-specific IgE. Asymptomatic sensitisation is common, so a positive result is meaningful only if it fits a corresponding clinical history. Never diagnose allergy or eliminate foods on a test alone.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: When should specific IgE (RAST) bloods be used instead of skin prick testing?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• When antihistamines cannot be stopped
  • in dermatographism or extensive skin disease (eczema)
  • high risk of anaphylaxis
  • or an uncooperative patient
Specific IgE is unaffected by antihistamines.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: How should a patient prepare for a skin prick test, and why?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Stop antihistamines 3–5 days beforehand, because they blunt the wheal response and cause false negatives. Perform only where resuscitation facilities are available.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for genuine diagnostic uncertainty in food or drug allergy?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: A supervised oral food/drug challenge. Component-resolved diagnostics (IgE to individual allergen proteins, e.g. Ara h 2) can further refine risk before challenge.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Which single serology result is the entry criterion for diagnosing ABPA?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Raised Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE (or a positive Aspergillus skin prick test) — an immediate type I hypersensitivity response.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What total IgE level is typically seen in active ABPA, and why is it measured serially?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Markedly raised, usually >1000 IU/mL. It is used to monitor disease activity and treatment response — falling with treatment, rising with relapse.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Why is a positive Aspergillus IgG/precipitin test NOT specific for ABPA?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Aspergillus IgG/precipitins (a type III response) also occur in chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma (mycetoma), so IgG alone does not confirm the allergic ABPA phenotype.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: In which two underlying conditions does ABPA classically arise, and what is the tell-tale sputum finding?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Asthma and cystic fibrosis. Patients classically cough up brownish mucus plugs, with fleeting CXR infiltrates and blood eosinophilia.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What is the mainstay of ABPA treatment, and what happens if it is left untreated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Oral corticosteroids are the mainstay (± itraconazole as an antifungal). Untreated ABPA progresses to central bronchiectasis and pulmonary fibrosis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Which four lymphocyte subsets does flow-cytometric immunophenotyping enumerate, and by which markers?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• CD4+ T-helper cells
  • CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
  • CD19/CD20+ B cells
  • and CD16/CD56+ NK cells

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: In HIV, what happens to the CD4 count and the CD4:CD8 ratio as disease progresses?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: CD4 count falls and CD8 rises, so the CD4:CD8 ratio inverts from the normal ~2:1 to <1.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: At what CD4 count is PCP prophylaxis indicated in HIV, and with what drug?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: CD4 <200 cells/µL (AIDS-defining threshold) — give Pneumocystis (PCP) prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: On ART, what does the CD4 count monitor versus the viral load?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• CD4 count monitors immune recovery (immune status)
  • viral load monitors virological response to treatment

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: How does the pattern of depleted subsets point to a primary immunodeficiency diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• Absent/low B cells → agammaglobulinaemia (X-linked/Bruton's)
  • low T cells → DiGeorge (thymic aplasia)
  • low T ± B ± NK → SCID (a paediatric emergency)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What is the underlying molecular defect in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: A defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes (neutrophils/macrophages), so they cannot generate the oxidative/respiratory burst (superoxide/reactive oxygen species) needed to kill ingested microbes. Most commonly X-linked.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: How does the NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test behave in a normal person vs in CGD?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• Normal neutrophils reduce yellow NBT to blue formazan (positive/blue)
  • In CGD the neutrophils cannot, so the dye stays yellow/colourless (abnormal/negative)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What is the DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test and why is it preferred over NBT?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
DHR flow cytometry measures the oxidative burst quantitatively:
  • normal neutrophils oxidise DHR to fluorescent rhodamine
  • CGD neutrophils show absent/reduced fluorescence
It is more sensitive and quantitative, and better detects carriers and residual-activity variants.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Which class of organisms causes infection in CGD, and give the two classic examples.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Catalase-positive organisms (they destroy their own peroxide so the phagocyte cannot borrow it). Classic examples: Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus (also Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Outline the management of CGD.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• Lifelong antibacterial prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) and antifungal prophylaxis (itraconazole)
  • interferon-gamma
  • definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What do vaccine (test-immunisation) antibody responses actually assess?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: The FUNCTION of the humoral (B-cell/antibody) immune system — whether the patient can mount a protective specific antibody response — not simply the level of total immunoglobulins. A test vaccine is given and specific titres are re-checked after ~4 weeks.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Why can total immunoglobulin levels be misleading in antibody deficiency?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Total IgG measures quantity, not quality. A patient can have near-normal total IgG yet fail to make functioning protective specific antibody — so a functional antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID, specific antibody deficiency) is missed unless you test the response to a vaccine. Function > level.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Contrast the two antigen types used in test immunisation and the immune response each probes.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• Protein antigen = tetanus/diphtheria toxoid → T-cell-DEPENDENT response
  • Polysaccharide antigen = unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide (PPV23) → T-cell-INDEPENDENT response

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: A patient responds normally to tetanus toxoid but fails to respond to unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide. Diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Specific (selective) polysaccharide antibody deficiency — isolated failure of the T-cell-independent anti-polysaccharide response with a normal protein (T-cell-dependent) response. Presents with recurrent infections by encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: Two key safety caveats when performing/interpreting test vaccination in suspected immunodeficiency?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
• 1) Do NOT interpret responses during immunosuppression (steroids, rituximab, chemotherapy blunt titres)
  • 2) Live vaccines are contraindicated in significant immunodeficiency — use only inactivated/toxoid and polysaccharide/conjugate vaccines for testing

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: What is the first-line antibody-arm test in suspected immunodeficiency, and how do you read it?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back:
Serum IgG/IgA/IgM.
  • All low = XLA/CVID
  • isolated low IgA = selective IgA deficiency
  • high IgM + low IgG/IgA = hyper-IgM
Then test function with vaccine responses.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: A patient has recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections. Which screen and what result?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Screen complement: CH50 (classical) and AH50 (alternative). Low CH50 and AH50 → a terminal-pathway (C5–C9/MAC) defect; vaccinate against meningococcus + prophylaxis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.front: How is SCID screened for before symptoms, and what is the golden rule in any new immunodeficiency?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__A.back: Newborn bloodspot TRECs (absent/low = absent T cells) → confirm with lymphocyte subsets. Always exclude HIV (secondary immunodeficiency) first in any new/unexplained case.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: In hepatitis B, what does isolated anti-HBs positivity (with negative HBsAg and negative anti-HBc) indicate?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Immunity from vaccination. The vaccine contains only surface antigen, so it generates anti-HBs alone — a negative anti-HBc confirms there was never natural infection.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A patient is anti-HBs positive AND anti-HBc positive, but HBsAg negative. Interpretation?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
Immunity following past, naturally cleared hepatitis B infection.
  • Presence of anti-HBc (core antibody) means true infection occurred
  • loss of HBsAg with gain of anti-HBs means it resolved

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What defines chronic hepatitis B, and which markers indicate high infectivity?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: HBsAg positive for more than 6 months (with anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative). High infectivity/replication is shown by HBeAg positivity and high HBV DNA.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A patient is anti-HCV antibody positive but HCV RNA (PCR) negative. What does this mean?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Past infection that has cleared (spontaneously or after treatment). Antibody reflects exposure; a negative RNA means no active viral replication.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Which is the UK first-line HIV screening test and why is it advantageous?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: The 4th-generation combined antigen/antibody assay, detecting p24 antigen plus anti-HIV antibody. Adding p24 antigen shortens the window period, so it turns positive earlier than antibody-only tests. Reactive results must be confirmed.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Contrast the acute versus past-infection serology in EBV and CMV.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• EBV: VCA IgM = acute; VCA IgG and EBNA IgG = past/immunity (screen with heterophile antibody test (Monospot / Paul-Bunnell))
  • CMV: IgM = acute, IgG = past
CMV causes heterophile-negative glandular fever and is dangerous in pregnancy, transplant and immunocompromise.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What type of immune response do the Mantoux test and IGRA detect?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: A cell-mediated, type IV (delayed-type) T-cell response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. They detect TB infection (usually latent TB) and cannot distinguish latent from active disease.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: In the Mantoux test, what is measured, and at what time?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: The diameter of induration (the palpable raised firm area) — NOT erythema — measured transversely at 48-72 hours after intradermal injection of tuberculin PPD.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Why is IGRA not confounded by prior BCG vaccination, whereas Mantoux is?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: IGRA uses M. tuberculosis-specific antigens ESAT-6 and CFP-10, which are absent from the BCG strain (and most non-tuberculous mycobacteria). BCG therefore does not produce a positive IGRA, while it commonly causes a false-positive Mantoux.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: List causes of a false-negative Mantoux test.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Immunosuppression
  • HIV
  • very young age
  • and miliary or overwhelming TB (anergy)
Any state impairing the cell-mediated response can blunt the reaction.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: A well, asymptomatic patient has a positive IGRA. What does this mean and what is the next step?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: It indicates latent TB infection. Manage by excluding active disease (clinical review, CXR) and considering chemoprophylaxis (e.g. isoniazid + rifampicin). A positive test alone does not diagnose active TB.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Which antibody target defines pemphigus vulgaris, and what level does the skin split at?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
Antibodies against desmoglein 3 (± desmoglein 1) at desmosomes, causing loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis) and an INTRA-epidermal split. Clinically:
  • flaccid blisters
  • painful erosions
  • prominent mucosal involvement
  • positive Nikolsky sign

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Which antigens are targeted in bullous pemphigoid, and where do they sit?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1) — hemidesmosome proteins at the dermo-epidermal junction/basement membrane. Antibodies cause a SUB-epidermal split → tense blisters in the elderly, mucosa usually spared, negative Nikolsky. Anti-BP180 correlates best with disease activity.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Contrast the direct immunofluorescence (DIF) patterns of pemphigus vs pemphigoid.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Pemphigus: intercellular IgG in a 'chicken-wire'/fishnet pattern between keratinocytes
  • Pemphigoid: linear IgG and C3 deposited along the basement membrane
DIF on perilesional skin is the gold-standard diagnostic test.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What is the Nikolsky sign and how does it differ between pemphigus and pemphigoid?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
Lateral pressure/shear on skin causes the epidermis to slough.
  • POSITIVE in pemphigus (weak intra-epidermal adhesion from acantholysis)
  • NEGATIVE in bullous pemphigoid (split is sub-epidermal, so the epidermis stays intact)

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What are serum anti-Dsg and anti-BP ELISA antibodies used for beyond diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: They confirm the target antigen (anti-Dsg1/3 in pemphigus, anti-BP180/BP230 in pemphigoid) and are used to MONITOR disease activity and predict relapse — anti-Dsg3 and anti-BP180 titres in particular track disease severity.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: Explain the two-tier syphilis serology algorithm.
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back:
• Treponemal test (EIA/TPPA) = screen, stays positive for life = exposure
  • Non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL) = a titre reflecting activity; a 4-fold fall = successful treatment

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What is the prozone effect in syphilis testing?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Very high antibody titres (e.g. secondary syphilis) can give a false-negative RPR/VDRL. The fix is to dilute the serum before re-testing.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: What does an isolated anti-HBc (HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative) result mean, and why does it matter?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Resolved infection with waned anti-HBs, occult HBV, or a false positive — check HBV DNA. It matters because of reactivation risk before immunosuppression/chemotherapy.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.front: How does dermatitis herpetiformis appear on direct immunofluorescence, and how is it treated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__I.back: Granular IgA in the dermal papillae (vs linear IgG/C3 in pemphigoid). It is coeliac-associated — check anti-tTG/anti-endomysial and treat with dapsone + gluten-free diet.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A 25-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgia and a positive ANA. Which antibody is most specific for SLE and correlates with activity?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity/lupus nephritis. ANA is sensitive but non-specific; anti-Sm is also highly specific but does not track activity.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with sinusitis, haemoptysis and rapidly progressive renal impairment is cANCA/anti-PR3 positive. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: cANCA/anti-PR3 with upper and lower respiratory involvement plus glomerulonephritis is classic GPA. pANCA/anti-MPO is associated with MPA and EGPA.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A middle-aged woman has cholestatic LFTs, pruritus and a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. What is the likely diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: AMA positivity with a cholestatic picture and pruritus in a middle-aged woman is characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A pregnant woman with Sjögren's syndrome is anti-Ro (SSA) positive. What is the main fetal risk to monitor for?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Anti-Ro (and anti-La) cross the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital complete heart block, so fetal cardiac monitoring is arranged.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with systemic sclerosis has widespread skin involvement and is anti-Scl-70 positive. Which complications is this subtype most associated with?
options: Lung fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis (diffuse disease)
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: Lung fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis (diffuse disease)
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse systemic sclerosis, which carries the risk of interstitial lung fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis. Anti-centromere marks limited disease (CREST) with a pulmonary hypertension risk.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with proximal muscle weakness, raised CK and interstitial lung disease is anti-Jo-1 positive. What is the underlying condition?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Anti-Jo-1 defines the antisynthetase syndrome — myositis with interstitial lung disease, mechanic's hands and Raynaud's.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with symmetrical small-joint synovitis and early-morning stiffness is anti-CCP positive. What does the anti-CCP add beyond diagnosis?
options: It indicates a worse prognosis (erosive disease), favouring earlier aggressive DMARDs
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: It indicates a worse prognosis (erosive disease), favouring earlier aggressive DMARDs
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Anti-CCP is specific for RA and prognostic — its positivity predicts erosive, extra-articular disease, supporting earlier, more aggressive treatment.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with Sjögren's syndrome and no joint symptoms has a strongly positive rheumatoid factor. How should this be interpreted?
options: RF is non-specific and high in Sjögren's — it does not diagnose RA on its own
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: RF is non-specific and high in Sjögren's — it does not diagnose RA on its own
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: RF is frequently positive (often high titre) in Sjögren's and other conditions. It cannot diagnose RA alone; correlate with the clinical picture and anti-CCP.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient has clear clinical rheumatoid arthritis but both RF and anti-CCP are negative. What is the correct conclusion?
options: This is seronegative RA — treat clinically with early DMARDs
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: This is seronegative RA — treat clinically with early DMARDs
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Around 20–30% of RA is seronegative. RA is a clinical diagnosis; negative serology does not exclude it and treatment should not be delayed.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A 30-year-old woman has had two unprovoked DVTs and three first-trimester miscarriages. Her APTT is prolonged and does not correct on mixing. What is the likely diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Thrombosis plus recurrent pregnancy loss with a lupus anticoagulant (prolonged APTT not correcting on mixing) is antiphospholipid syndrome — confirm with persistent antibodies ≥12 weeks apart.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: How should a pregnant woman with antiphospholipid syndrome and prior pregnancy loss be managed?
options: Aspirin alone in the third trimester
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: In pregnancy, APS is managed with aspirin and LMWH (warfarin is teratogenic and avoided). This reduces pregnancy loss and thrombosis risk.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: Which laboratory finding is characteristically paradoxical in antiphospholipid syndrome?
options: A prolonged PT that corrects on mixing
A prolonged APTT (lupus anticoagulant) despite a prothrombotic tendency
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: A prolonged APTT (lupus anticoagulant) despite a prothrombotic tendency
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: The lupus anticoagulant prolongs the APTT in vitro but causes clotting in vivo — a classic paradox; it does not correct on mixing with normal plasma.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient with SLE presents with a flare of nephritis. Which complement pattern is expected and what does it reflect?
options: High C3 and C4 — inactive disease
Low C3 and C4 — complement consumption tracking disease activity
Low C3 with normal C4 — post-streptococcal GN
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: Low C3 and C4 — complement consumption tracking disease activity
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Active SLE consumes complement via the classical/immune-complex pathway, lowering C3 and C4; the levels fall with flares (especially nephritis) and recover with treatment.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A young adult has had two episodes of meningococcal meningitis. Which immune abnormality should be investigated?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections are the hallmark of terminal complement deficiency — screen with CH50 and vaccinate against meningococcus.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.question: A patient has recurrent episodes of facial and airway swelling WITHOUT urticaria that do not respond to adrenaline or antihistamines; C4 is persistently low. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
options: Hereditary angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency) — give C1-inhibitor concentrate
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.answer: Hereditary angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency) — give C1-inhibitor concentrate
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__C.explanation: Angioedema without urticaria, unresponsive to adrenaline/antihistamines, with a low C4, is hereditary angioedema. It is treated with C1-inhibitor concentrate (or bradykinin-targeted agents), not the anaphylaxis pathway.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain that is worse in the morning and improves with exercise; MRI shows sacroiliitis and he is HLA-B27 positive. What is the likely diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Young-onset inflammatory back pain with MRI sacroiliitis and HLA-B27 positivity is axial spondyloarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis (the strongest HLA-B27 association).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A healthy blood donor is found to be HLA-B27 positive on incidental testing, with no symptoms. What does this mean?
options: Nothing on its own — HLA-B27 occurs in ~8% of healthy people and only supports a diagnosis in the right clinical context
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.answer: Nothing on its own — HLA-B27 occurs in ~8% of healthy people and only supports a diagnosis in the right clinical context
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: HLA-B27 is common in the general population; a positive result in an asymptomatic person is not diagnostic and needs clinical correlation.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A young man develops asymmetrical lower-limb arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis two weeks after an episode of dysentery. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: The post-infective triad of arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis is reactive arthritis — an HLA-B27-associated spondyloarthropathy.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A 28-year-old from Turkey has recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers, an episode of uveitis, and develops a pustule at a venepuncture site. Which HLA allele is associated with this condition?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Recurrent oral/genital ulcers, uveitis and a positive pathergy reaction (the pustule) in someone from the Silk Road is Behçet's disease, associated with HLA-B51.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: What does a positive pathergy test represent in Behçet's disease?
options: Skin hyper-reactivity — a papule/pustule forming after a needle prick
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.answer: Skin hyper-reactivity — a papule/pustule forming after a needle prick
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Pathergy is non-specific skin hyper-reactivity where a sterile pustule forms after minor skin trauma (needle prick) — characteristic of Behçet's disease.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: Which complication of Behçet's disease is sight-threatening and needs urgent specialist input?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Behçet's posterior or panuveitis can rapidly threaten sight and, along with neuro-Behçet's and large-vessel disease, requires urgent specialist assessment and immunosuppression.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: Which HLA allele is classically associated with hereditary haemochromatosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: HLA-A3 is the classic association with hereditary haemochromatosis (linked to the HFE gene). B27 → spondyloarthropathy; DR4 → RA; DQ2 → coeliac; Cw6 → psoriasis.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A patient with suspected coeliac disease has a negative HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8. How does this help?
options: It makes coeliac disease very unlikely (high negative predictive value)
It indicates the patient must avoid gluten
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.answer: It makes coeliac disease very unlikely (high negative predictive value)
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Coeliac disease is almost universally DQ2/DQ8 positive, so a negative result has a high NPV and effectively excludes it — the test's main clinical use.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: Which HLA combination confers the highest risk of type 1 diabetes?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Co-inheritance of HLA-DR3 and DR4 confers the highest genetic risk of type 1 diabetes.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: Minutes after a kidney transplant is reperfused, the graft becomes mottled and thromboses. What type of rejection is this and what causes it?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes-hours due to preformed antibodies against donor ABO/HLA antigens, causing thrombosis. It is prevented by the pre-transplant cross-match, not treated.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A prospective transplant recipient has a POSITIVE cross-match against a potential donor. What does this indicate?
options: This donor is contraindicated — high risk of hyperacute rejection
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.answer: This donor is contraindicated — high risk of hyperacute rejection
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: A positive cross-match means the recipient has preformed antibodies against that donor's HLA — transplanting would risk hyperacute rejection, so the donor is avoided.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: A transplant candidate has a very high panel reactive antibody (PRA). What does this imply?
options: They are highly sensitised and harder to find a compatible donor
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.answer: They are highly sensitised and harder to find a compatible donor
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: A high PRA means the recipient has HLA antibodies against a large proportion of the population (from prior sensitising events), making a negative cross-match harder to achieve.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.question: Before starting abacavir for HIV, which test should be checked to avoid a severe hypersensitivity reaction?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__R.explanation: HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity, so it is screened before prescribing and a positive result contraindicates the drug. HLA-B27 = spondyloarthropathy, DQ2/DQ8 = coeliac, DR4 = rheumatoid arthritis, B51 = Behçet's.

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.question: A woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day and after reading. Anti-AChR antibodies are positive. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.explanation: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia worsening with activity, with positive anti-AChR antibodies, is myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic NMJ disorder).

investigations__IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__N.question: A myasthenic patient becomes increasingly breathless with a falling forced vital capacity and bulbar weakness. What is the priority management?
